CHAPTER 1 — THE FIRST VICTORY

ONE IN A MILLION

Before Joshua was a leader in Canaan, he was a servant in the wilderness. He was born into Egyptian slavery, endured Pharaoh’s harsh rule, and witnessed the mighty hand of God bring plagues, part seas, and preserve a nation. He saw water gush from a rock and manna fall from heaven. He watched the Red Sea swallow the Egyptian army—and then he watched nearly all of his generation fall in the wilderness. Among two million Israelites, only two men who left Egypt would live to step foot in the Promised Land: Caleb and Joshua. Joshua was literally one in a million.

You, too, are special. You were miraculously created by Almighty God. He has a special plan and purpose for your life. He loves you. To be loved by God is life’s highest calling and greatest achievement! You are called into a love relationship with God. He knows you and wishes to reveal Himself to you and fellowship with you. Satan wants to tell you a different story. He wants to feed you the lie that you are insignificant, unloved, and useless. He whispers the false truth that God has betrayed you, abandoned you, and has left you to figure life out on your own. Satan offers false hope in substance abuse, illicit relationships, and countless other distractions to numb your doubts, questions, and pain. However, the truth is that none of this will help. Only Jesus can satisfy your soul.

Before reading any further, I challenge you to turn your heart toward God. Settle in your heart that, regardless of your current situation, God has forever proved His love for you by sending His Son, Jesus Christ, to die on the cross. (John 3:16, Romans 8:32) Accept that no matter your age, race, gender, social status, Spiritual maturity, or past, God loves you, He accepts you, and in Him, you are secure and significant! Without settling these truths in your mind, heart, and soul, the remainder of this book will be only empty words, unhelpful quotes, and unheeded Scriptures. But with the love of God in your heart, I pray this book will strengthen your faith, encourage your spirit, and renew your resolve to follow God. He will guide you into great victory, and you, like Joshua, will be one in a million!

❝ Joshua was literally one in a million ❞

FROM COMPLAINT TO COMBAT

The first time Joshua appears in Scripture, it’s not as a general, a prophet, or a miracle worker—it’s as a young man given a nearly impossible assignment: fight Amalek. (Deuteronomy 1:35-38, Numbers 14:30) Israel had just received water from a rock in Rephidim. The people had once again accused Moses of trying to kill them. Despite miracle after miracle, they questioned whether the Lord was even among them. “Wherefore the people did chide with Moses, and said, Give us water that we may drink. And Moses said unto them, Why chide ye with me? wherefore do ye tempt the LORD?” (Exodus 17:2) “...Is the LORD among us, or not?” (Exodus 17:7) (1 Corinthians 10:1–5)

What should have been a moment of worship became a place of complaint. And in that spiritual vulnerability, the enemy attacked. Amalek seemingly came out of nowhere, at Israel’s most vulnerable moment. Amalek was a desert-dwelling nation, descended from Esau. They were not strangers to Israel, nor were they random aggressors. Again and again throughout Scripture, Amalek represents the flesh—the part of us that rebels against God, resents surrender, and resists obedience. (Galatians 5:16-17, Romans 7:18-25) Israel had just questioned God’s presence—“Is the LORD among us or not?”—and right then, Amalek launched an assault. Their timing wasn’t random. The flesh always fights hardest when faith is weakest.

In 2022, I became a new pastor. It was the great joy and privilege of my life. Shortly thereafter, I was tempted to discontinue a youth camp our church had hosted for many years. It was at this camp, in fact, that I surrendered my life to God as a young man. But in this season, I wanted to quit - not because of the work involved, the financial undertaking it was to the church, or the great amount of time and preparation it required to host camp. No, I wanted to quit because I had little faith that God could use some of the people involved. It is embarrassing to look back on the prideful attitude I had at that moment. But I was convinced I knew better than everyone else. Rather than attempting to work through several differences, my self-centeredness said, “You don’t need them, you are more Spiritual than they are, give in and give it up.”

Praise God for the wise advice of a Godly friend that convinced me not to throw away what God had given me to steward. Over the past few years, God has used this camp to draw many young people to Himself for salvation. Others have come to receive help and healing. These life-changing decisions were made at a camp I wanted to discontinue. My fleshly pride reared its ugly head and nearly convinced me that even God could not use His own people. The flesh always fights hardest when faith is weakest.

When Amalek came, Moses turned to Joshua. “Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim. And Moses said unto Joshua, Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek: to morrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand.” (Exodus 17:8–9) Israel had no trained soldiers. Joshua was not a trained military leader; he had likely spent his youth as a brickmaker in Egypt. Yet without protest, Joshua obeyed. “So Joshua did as Moses had said to him, and fought with Amalek.” (Exodus 17:10) There were no excuses. No delay. No strategy meeting or crisis of confidence. He simply obeyed. His courage didn’t come from his experience—it came from Almighty God.

❝ The flesh always fights hardest when faith is weakest ❞

THE HILL AND THE SWORD

While Joshua led the battle in the valley, Moses ascended a hill with the rod of God in his hand. As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed. But when his hands dropped, Amalek gained ground. “And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.” (Exodus 17:11) (1 Timothy 2:8)  So Aaron and Hur came beside him. They found him a seat. Then, one on each side, they held up his arms—steady until the setting of the sun. “And Moses’ hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.” (Exodus 17:12) (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, Galatians 6:2) This is the Scriptural pattern of spiritual victory: prayer, another obedience, and support from the body of Christ. It wasn’t Joshua’s sword, Moses’ rod, or Aaron and Hur’s support system that won the battle. It was God. All the glory belonged to the Lord.

A MEMORIAL AND A MESSAGE

After the battle, God commanded Moses to record what had happened. He was to rehearse it in the ears of Joshua. “And the LORD said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.” (Exodus 17:14) God didn’t want Joshua to remember the fight—He wanted him to remember Who had fought for him.

As a child, I would often wrestle with my dad. I think every six-year-old boy is convinced he can take his “old man” and needs a reminder from time to time that he can’t. Often my dad would say, “Who’s your daddy?” This usually came after tickling us until we screamed like a dying rabbit or tossing us around the living room like a rag doll - Smack! Bam! Wham! “Who’s your daddy?” In a playful way, my dad was reminding us, not about the fight, but who was in charge and who was going to win every time. God wanted Joshua to remember who his “Daddy” was - it was Jehovah God. God would fight for Joshua, and God would win every time!

Moses then built an altar and named it Jehovahnissi: “The Lord is my banner.” “And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it Jehovahnissi: For he said, Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.” (Exodus 17:15–16) (Psalm 20:5, 1 Samuel 7:12) That altar marked the moment when a man, who had never led an army, obeyed God, had fearless faith in Him, and witnessed the power of Heaven working through his obedience.

FOUR LESSONS FROM THE FIRST VICTORY

1. Don’t Indulge in Self-Pity Israel was quick to complain when things went wrong: “No food? No water? No army? God has failed us!” But Joshua’s heart said: “No food? No water? No army? No problem! God has never failed us.” We do ourselves no good when we wallow in fear or resentment. God’s provision may still come, but that doesn’t mean He is pleased with our attitude. Don’t confuse the goodness of God in your life as His approval of your poor behavior. Water gushed from the rock, but God was grieved. (Psalm 78:15-22, Lamentations 3:22-23)

2. The Word of the Lord Will Battle Amalek Amalek—the old man, the flesh—will not rest. There will be no ceasefire in this spiritual war. But the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, will always cut through. “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.” (Hebrews 4:12) (Ephesians 6:17, Matthew 4:1-11)

3. What God Commands, Undertake Immediately Joshua didn’t hesitate. He obeyed the moment the instruction came. This is true faith: not debating, not stalling, but stepping into God’s assignment—even when it feels impossible. “Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.” (John 2:5) (Luke 5:5, James 1:22) God-sized tasks require faith.

4. God Gives Power to Those Who Call on Him Victory in the valley came because of intercession on the hill. Moses couldn’t do it alone. He needed help to keep calling on God. That picture is a reminder to every believer: we are stronger together. When the body of Christ supports each other in prayer, when hands are held up and faith is steady, God works. “Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.” (Jeremiah 33:3) (Matthew 18:19-20, Colossians 4:2)

I recently went through a season of temptation. Every time I stepped foot in a specific location I would be bombarded with the same temptation. “That is simple,” you might say, “stop going to the place you are tempted.” I would usually agree with you. However, this was happening in the new home my wife and I had just purchased. There was no going back. It was a done deal, and the temptations would not stop.

I had two choices: 1. Keep this to myself and attempt to fight alone. I knew this would ultimately lead to failure and sin. 2. Call in backup. Thank God I had the sense to go with option two. I explained the situation to several men of our church, a few pastor friends, and my wife. I asked them to pray that this specific temptation would cease and God would protect our new home from the lies of the enemy. The temptations stopped immediately when they prayed!

Satan wanted to condemn me for being tempted. He wanted to isolate me away from my family and the people of God and make me feel as though I had already sinned. It is not a sin to be tempted - if it is a sin to be tempted, then Jesus was a sinner because He was tempted by Satan. However, it is a sin to dwell upon and act on that temptation.

I was in a battle for my Spiritual life. My hands were weary. I am so grateful for Aarons and Hurs that did not throw me away for being in battle with the enemy, but held up my hands in prayer to God. Victory in the valley came because of intercession on the hill.

❝ Victory in the valley came because of intercession on the hill ❞

THE BATTLE BELONGS TO THE LORD

Who won the battle? Was it Joshua with the sword? Moses with the rod? Aaron and Hur with their support? No. The honor belongs to God alone. He gave the strength. He brought the victory. “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.” (Proverbs 21:31) (2 Chronicles 20:15, Psalm 44:3, Romans 8:37). The same is true for us. Our calling is not to conquer in our own might, but to obey, pray, and trust. The Lord who delivered Israel at Rephidim is still fighting for His people today. And like Joshua, our victories begin with simple, courageous obedience.

Meditative Thoughts:

• Where in your life have you been tempted to say, “Is the Lord among us or not?” How has He already shown

Himself faithful?

• Are there moments when you’ve allowed self-pity or complaint to take root instead of trust?

• Who are the Aarons and Hurs in your life—those who hold up your hands in prayer when you’re weary? Do you thank God for them? Are you Aaron and Hur for anyone?

• What seemingly impossible assignment has God given you right now? What would obedience today look like?

• Can you name a memorial in your life—a moment you can point to and say, “God fought for me there”?

Let these reflections settle in your heart as reminders that victory begins not with power, but with faith-filled obedience.
